claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 7B, C and Table 6.

claims.claim: Removal of BMK-1 function abolished microtubule reorganization and prevented chromosome segregation following monopole breakdown.
claims.source: This suggested that removal of BMK-1 function abolished microtubule reorganization and prevented chromosome segregation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of mini anaphases in the bmk-1(ok391) background.

claims.claim: In klp-18(RNAi), bmk-1(syb3914) worms in the absence of auxin, monopolar spindles formed and then chromosomes moved back towards the pole in a manner indistinguishable from normal monopolar anaphase.
claims.source: To confirm this result, we generated a version of our Dynein AID live imaging strain (expressing GFP::tubulin and GFP::histone to visualize the spindle) containing the bmk-1(syb3914) deletion and performed acute dynein depletion coupled with ex utero imaging to determine if mini anaphases could still form. In klp-18(RNAi), bmk-1(syb3914) worms in the absence of auxin, monopolar spindles formed and then chromosomes moved back towards the pole in a manner indistinguishable from normal monopolar anaphase (Video 15, n = 4).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Video 15.

claims.claim: When auxin was added to deplete dynein in klp-18(RNAi), bmk-1(syb3914) worms, monopolar spindles broke down as expected and individual chromosomes remained associated with microtubule bundles, but there were no signs of segregation.
claims.source: When auxin was added to deplete dynein, monopolar spindles broke down as expected and individual chromosomes remained associated with microtubule bundles. However, as time elapsed, there were no signs of segregation, microtubule density decreased, and chromosomes remained in the cytoplasm with no discernible anaphase spindles forming (Figure 7D, Video 16, n = 3).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 7D and Video 16.

claims.claim: BMK-1 provides outward sorting force on microtubules during oocyte meiosis, redundant to the forces produced by KLP-18.
claims.source: These data support the hypothesis that BMK-1 provides outward sorting force on microtubules during oocyte meiosis, redundant to the forces produced by KLP-18.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings with bmk-1 mutants.

claims.claim: Dynein activity is required throughout the meiotic divisions to establish and maintain focused poles.
claims.source: Collectively, these data have contributed to a more complete model for how acentrosomal spindles are assembled and stabilized during oocyte meiosis (Figure 8). Dynein activity is required throughout the meiotic divisions to establish and maintain focused poles, and its removal via acute AID generated spindle defects within minutes.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Removal of dynein via acute AID generated spindle defects within minutes.
claims.source: Dynein activity is required throughout the meiotic divisions to establish and maintain focused poles, and its removal via acute AID generated spindle defects within minutes.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from acute AID experiments.

claims.claim: Dynein depletion increased the length of bipolar oocyte spindles.
claims.source: Dynein depletion increased the length of bipolar oocyte spindles and led to increased dispersion of microtubule minus ends across the spindle.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Dynein depletion led to increased dispersion of microtubule minus ends across the spindle.
claims.source: Dynein depletion increased the length of bipolar oocyte spindles and led to increased dispersion of microtubule minus ends across the spindle.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: When performing dynein depletions on a monopolar spindle, the monopole completely broke apart and microtubule bundles were ejected into the cytoplasm.
claims.source: When performing these depletions on a monopolar spindle, the monopole completely broke apart and microtubule bundles were ejected into the cytoplasm.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claims.claim: Dynein is required to stitch minus ends together into a stable pole structure.
claims.source: Together, these findings demonstrate that dynein is required to stitch minus ends together into a stable pole structure.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on all the dynein depletion experiments.

claims.claim: After the monopole disassembled, microtubules were able to reorganize into a 'miniature' spindle.
claims.source: Remarkably, we also found that after the monopole disassembled, microtubules were able to reorganize into a 'miniature' spindle; chromosomes then segregated on these spindles in the absence of dynein.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claims.claim: Chromosomes segregated on miniature spindles in the absence of dynein.
claims.source: Remarkably, we also found that after the monopole disassembled, microtubules were able to reorganize into a 'miniature' spindle; chromosomes then segregated on these spindles in the absence of dynein.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claims.claim: The finding that chromosomes segregate on miniature spindles seemingly contradicts a previous study where dynein was proposed to drive chromosomes towards poles along laterally associated microtubule bundles.
claims.source: This finding seemingly contradicts one of our previous studies, where we proposed that dynein could drive chromosomes towards poles along laterally associated microtubule bundles, representing a type of 'anaphase A' segregation mechanism (Muscat et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a discussion of how the current findings relate to previous work.

claims.claim: Dynein was a good candidate for driving chromosomes towards poles since it provided chromosomes with a minus-end-directed force prior to anaphase.
claims.source: Dynein was a good candidate for such a role since we found that it provided chromosomes with a minus-end-directed force prior to anaphase, and we observed lagging chromosomes in anaphase following dynein inhibition (Muscat et al., 2015); lagging chromosomes upon dynein depletion have also been reported by others (McNally et al., 2016) and were observed in the current study (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is a discussion of previous findings and their interpretation.

claims.claim: Lagging chromosomes were observed in anaphase following dynein inhibition.
claims.source: Dynein was a good candidate for such a role since we found that it provided chromosomes with a minus-end-directed force prior to anaphase, and we observed lagging chromosomes in anaphase following dynein inhibition (Muscat et al., 2015); lagging chromosomes upon dynein depletion have also been reported by others (McNally et al., 2016) and were observed in the current study (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Muscat et al., 2015 and McNally et al., 2016, and by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Anaphase-B-like mechanism is the major driver of chromosome segregation in C. elegans oocytes.
claims.source: Indeed, in subsequent years it has become clear that this anaphase-B-like mechanism is the major driver of chromosome segregation in C. elegans oocytes, and that anaphase A chromosome-to-pole movement provides only a minor contribution (McNally et al., 2016; Laband et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to McNally et al., 2016 and Laband et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Anaphase A chromosome-to-pole movement provides only a minor contribution to chromosome segregation in C. elegans oocytes.
claims.source: Indeed, in subsequent years it has become clear that this anaphase-B-like mechanism is the major driver of chromosome segregation in C. elegans oocytes, and that anaphase A chromosome-to-pole movement provides only a minor contribution (McNally et al., 2016; Laband et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to McNally et al., 2016 and Laband et al., 2017.

claims.claim: If dynein plays a role in chromosome segregation, its contribution is redundant with other, more dominant, mechanisms.
claims.source: Given these follow-up studies, it is now clear that if dynein plays a role in chromosome segregation, its contribution is redundant with other, more dominant, mechanisms; this would explain why most chromosomes were able to move poleward following dynein inhibition in our original study and in subsequent studies by other labs (Muscat et al., 2015; McNally et al., 2016; Laband et al., 2017; Danlasky et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the current findings and previous studies cited.

claims.claim: Anaphase-B-like spindle elongation can occur in the absence of KLP-18.
claims.source: Although it is possible that KLP-18 may contribute to outward sliding of microtubules during wild-type anaphase, our work shows that this motor is not absolutely required for anaphase spindle elongation and demonstrates that there must be other factors that can perform this function.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation of mini anaphases in the absence of KLP-18.

claims.claim: There must be other factors besides KLP-18 that can perform anaphase spindle elongation.
claims.source: Although it is possible that KLP-18 may contribute to outward sliding of microtubules during wild-type anaphase, our work shows that this motor is not absolutely required for anaphase spindle elongation and demonstrates that there must be other factors that can perform this function.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of mini anaphases in the absence of KLP-18.

claims.claim: Loss of dynein activity had strong phenotypes that manifested rapidly, within 2 min of auxin treatment.
claims.source: Our work also accentuates the importance of balanced forces within a bipolar meiotic spindle; we found that loss of dynein activity had strong phenotypes that manifested rapidly, within 2 min of auxin treatment.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from acute AID experiments.

claims.claim: Acute dynein depletion caused spindle lengthening, suggesting that dynein may normally provide an inward force on the spindle.
claims.source: Notably, acute dynein depletion caused spindle lengthening, suggesting that dynein may normally provide an inward force on the spindle, as has been demonstrated in previous studies of mitosis (Ferenz et al., 2009; van Heesbeen et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the spindle lengthening data and is consistent with previous studies cited.

claims.claim: Inactivation of KLP-18 in stable, bipolar spindles caused spindle shortening followed by collapse of microtubule minus ends into a monopolar spindle.
claims.source: Recently, our lab also demonstrated that inactivation of KLP-18 in stable, bipolar spindles caused spindle shortening followed by collapse of microtubule minus ends into a monopolar spindle (Wolff et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Wolff et al., 2021.

claims.claim: The collapse of bipolar spindles into monopolar spindles upon KLP-18 inactivation is due to a loss of the outward force provided by KLP-18.
claims.source: This collapse is due to a loss of the outward force provided by KLP-18, theoretically enabling the inward force provided by dynein to dominate and highlighting how quickly an imbalance of these motor forces can lead to gross defects in spindle organization.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings from Wolff et al., 2021.

claims.claim: An imbalance of motor forces can quickly lead to gross defects in spindle organization.

claims.evidence: This is a general conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: KLP-18/kinesin-12 provides the major outward force in C. elegans oocyte meiosis.
claims.source: While KLP-18/kinesin-12 provides the major outward force in C. elegans oocyte meiosis (Wolff et al., 2016), this critical function is performed by kinesin-5 in mouse oocytes (Schuh and Ellenberg, 2007) and in mitosis in many organisms (reviewed in Mann and Wadsworth, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Wolff et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Kinesin-5 provides the major outward force in mouse oocytes.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Schuh and Ellenberg, 2007.

claims.claim: Kinesin-5 provides the major outward force in mitosis in many organisms.
claims.source: While KLP-18/kinesin-12 provides the major outward force in C. elegans oocyte meiosis (Wolff et al., 2016), this critical function is performed by kinesin-5 in mouse oocytes (Schuh and Ellenberg, 2007) and in mitosis in many organisms (reviewed in Mann and Wadsworth, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a review by Mann and Wadsworth, 2019.

claims.source: Previous studies have shown that dynein and kinesin-5 antagonize each other in these organisms; inhibition of both motors simultaneously enables bipolar spindle formation (Mitchison et al., 2005; Tanenbaum et al., 2008; Ferenz et al., 2009; van Heesbeen et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Mitchison et al., 2005; Tanenbaum et al., 2008; Ferenz et al., 2009; and van Heesbeen et al., 2014.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Tanenbaum et al., 2009; Vanneste et al., 2009; Raaijmakers et al., 2012; Sturgill and Ohi, 2013; and Sturgill et al., 2016.

claims.claim: The roles of kinesin-5 and kinesin-12 have been seemingly switched between different organisms.

claims.claim: Different groups of proteins work in parallel to form and stabilize acentrosomal poles.
claims.source: Rather than all pole proteins interacting as a cohesive, cross-linked network around microtubule minus ends, it seems more plausible that different groups of proteins work in parallel to form and stabilize acentrosomal poles.

results.result: The auxin-inducible degron (AID) system was optimized in C. elegans to enable rapid depletion of dynein from oocyte spindles within minutes. The Dynein AID strain appears wild-type in the absence of auxin, and 4-hour auxin treatment results in undetectable dynein levels in mitotic embryos with expected phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6 and C45-C48 collectively demonstrate successful optimization and validation of the AID system. The strain shows no developmental defects without auxin (C45-C46), and auxin treatment depletes dynein within the expected timeframe (C6) with canonical mitotic phenotypes (C47-C48). Control experiments with the TIR1 control strain (C57) further validate specificity.

results.result: Dynein is required to maintain the integrity of acentrosomal poles during spindle assembly. Long-term dynein depletion causes pole splaying in 69.4% of spindles, with microtubule minus ends failing to coalesce, and this phenotype is dependent on dynein localization to poles.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8 and C53-C56 provide quantitative evidence from germline counting and IF imaging showing consistent pole splaying phenotypes. Claims C58-C60 demonstrate that delocalization of dynein via ASPM-1 or LIN-5 depletion produces identical phenotypes, confirming that pole localization is necessary for dynein function. The conclusion (C74) is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Acute dynein depletion from pre-formed metaphase spindles causes rapid pole splaying within 2-3 minutes, increases spindle length by ~3.5 μm, and disperses ASPM-1 across the spindle, while maintaining chromosome-microtubule associations and spindle bipolarity.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C73 provide comprehensive evidence from both fixed and live imaging showing rapid phenotypes upon acute dynein depletion. The ~50% increase in pole-to-equator ratio (C62), spindle lengthening (C67), and ASPM-1 dispersion (C65-C66) are quantified. Control experiments with TIR1 control strain (C72) and unarrested spindles (C64, C73) validate specificity and generality of the phenotype.

results.result: Dynein depletion from monopolar spindles (induced by KLP-18 depletion) causes catastrophic breakdown of the monopole, ejecting chromosomes with associated microtubule bundles into the cytoplasm. This demonstrates dynein's essential role in maintaining pole integrity and suggests the overlap zone stabilizes bipolar spindles.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10 and C75-C82 provide strong evidence from both long-term and acute AID experiments showing monopole breakdown. The phenotype is observed in 92.8% of oocytes (C76) and confirmed by live imaging (C81). The cone-shaped microtubule structures (C79) are described, though the interpretation about minus end coalescence (C80) is speculative. The conclusion about pole integrity (C83) and overlap zone stabilization (C84) is reasonably inferred from comparing bipolar and monopolar phenotypes.

results.result: Following monopole breakdown, individual chromosomes reorganize local microtubules and establish miniature bipolar spindles that mediate chromosome segregation. These mini anaphases segregate chromosomes to similar distances as wild-type (~5 μm) but not as far as dynein-depleted bipolar spindles (~6.5 μm).
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C12 and C86-C91 describe a striking and unexpected phenotype observed in live imaging (n=5). The synchronous, bidirectional chromosome movement (C87-C88) and quantified segregation distances (C90-C91) provide strong evidence. The inference that neither KLP-18 nor dynein is absolutely required for segregation (C89) is well-supported. The speculation about KLP-18's role in spindle elongation (C92) is appropriately cautious.

results.result: Miniature anaphase spindles recapitulate key hallmarks of normal anaphase, including lateral microtubule bundles in early anaphase, central microtubule localization in late anaphase, proper SUMO-marked ring complex behavior, and correct SEP-1 (separase) localization dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C96 describe microtubule organization patterns in mini anaphases from fixed imaging. Claims C97-C99 show SUMO localization in 93/93 oocytes, and C100-C103 show SEP-1 localization in 81/81 oocytes, both matching normal anaphase patterns. The conclusion (C104) that mini spindles recapitulate normal anaphase is well-supported by multiple independent markers.

results.result: Microtubules reorganize into bipolar structures around individual chromosomes following monopole breakdown. ASPM-1 localization suggests a transitional reorganization period, and SPD-1 localization between segregating chromosomes (122/122 oocytes) demonstrates antiparallel microtubule overlap in mini spindles.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C107 present the hypothesis and limited evidence (n=3) for transitional reorganization based on ASPM-1 localization. Claims C108-C112 provide strong evidence from SPD-1 localization in 122/122 oocytes showing antiparallel overlap. The conclusion (C113) about microtubule reorganization is well-supported, though the ASPM-1 data is limited and the transitional state is rarely captured.

results.result: The kinesin-5 motor BMK-1 provides redundant outward microtubule sorting force that enables mini spindle formation in the absence of KLP-18 and dynein. BMK-1 localizes to microtubules under all conditions (150/150 oocytes), and its removal prevents mini anaphase formation (0/164 oocytes in bmk-1(ok391); confirmed in bmk-1(syb3914)).
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C16 and C115-C129 provide strong evidence for BMK-1's role. BMK-1 localizes to microtubules in all conditions including monopole breakdown (C121-C123). Loss of BMK-1 completely abolishes mini anaphase formation in both deletion alleles (C124, C127-C128), while monopole breakdown still occurs (C125). This represents the first evidence for kinesin-5 contribution to C. elegans meiotic spindle organization (C16), which is a significant finding given prior reports of no major phenotypes (C117-C119).

results.result: The formation of miniature bipolar spindles reveals redundant microtubule sorting forces that are undetectable when KLP-18 and dynein are active, providing a unique opportunity to probe for masked motor forces.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C14 and C114 present the key conceptual framework for discovering BMK-1's role. The inference that redundant forces exist is well-supported by the experimental observation of mini spindle formation (C11-C12) and the subsequent identification of BMK-1 as providing this force (C15, C129). This represents an important insight into spindle organization.

results.result: Multiple motors (dynein, KLP-18, BMK-1) work synchronously to establish and maintain acentrosomal spindle bipolarity. Dynein provides inward force and pole focusing, KLP-18 provides major outward force, and BMK-1 provides redundant outward force. Imbalance of these forces quickly leads to spindle defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C17 and C130-C137 summarize the overall model supported by all experimental findings. The conclusion about multiple motors working synchronously (C17) integrates findings about dynein's role in pole integrity (C135), microtubule reorganization after monopole breakdown (C136-C137), and BMK-1's redundant function (C157). The statement about force balance (C150) is supported by the rapid phenotypes observed and comparison to prior work on KLP-18 inactivation (C148-C149).

results.result: Background context: Centrosomes organize mitotic spindle poles, but oocyte meiosis occurs without centrosomes. Acentrosomal spindles in human oocytes are frequently unstable, with poles splitting and rejoining, leading to high rates of chromosome segregation errors.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 and C18-C20 provide established background knowledge supported by citations (particularly Holubcová et al., 2015 for human oocyte instability). These claims establish the biological context and motivation for the study but do not represent new findings from this work.

results.result: Background on C. elegans oocyte spindle assembly: Microtubules nucleate near the nuclear envelope, KLP-18 pushes minus ends to form multiple poles that coalesce into a bipolar structure, the spindle rotates and shortens before anaphase, and various MAPs and motors (ASPM-1, KLP-7, MEI-1/2) contribute to assembly. Katanin is essential for spindle maintenance.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C33 describe the known process of spindle assembly in C. elegans oocytes, supported by multiple citations (Wolff et al., 2016; Gigant et al., 2017; Albertson and Thomson, 1993; Connolly et al., 2014, 2015; Srayko et al., 2000; McNally et al., 2014). These provide essential background but are not new findings.

results.result: Background on dynein function: In mitosis and other systems, dynein is required for pole focusing, centrosome anchoring, and poleward flux. In Xenopus, dynein inhibition causes splayed poles. In mouse oocytes, dynein is required for early spindle assembly. In C. elegans, dynein is crucial for spindle positioning and rotation, and its depletion causes longer spindles with pole defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C44 summarize prior work on dynein function across multiple systems, supported by numerous citations. These establish the rationale for studying dynein in C. elegans oocytes but represent prior knowledge rather than new findings from this study.

results.result: Validation of Dynein AID strain: Tagged dynein localizes to oocyte spindles with enrichment at poles during anaphase, consistent with previous studies. Live imaging confirms this pattern and reveals a kinetochore population.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C52 validate the Dynein AID strain by showing that tagged dynein localizes correctly (Figure 1C, Video 1, n=3), consistent with prior studies (Ellefson and McNally, 2009; van der Voet et al., 2009; McNally et al., 2016; Danlasky et al., 2020). This is important methodological validation but not a primary finding.

results.result: ASPM-1 and LIN-5 depletion produces pole splaying phenotypes nearly identical to Dynein AID (64-70%), and co-depletion with dynein does not worsen phenotypes. This confirms these proteins function in a single pathway by directing dynein localization to poles.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C59 and C162-C165 show that ASPM-1 and LIN-5 depletion phenocopy dynein depletion with similar frequencies (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Table 4), and co-depletion shows no additive effects. This supports the conclusion that these proteins function in a single pathway (C165), though the inference about a cross-linked network versus parallel pathways is discussed as uncertain in the manuscript.

results.result: Discussion of prior work: The current findings clarify that anaphase-B-like spindle elongation is the major driver of chromosome segregation in C. elegans oocytes, with dynein playing at most a minor, redundant role. KLP-18 is not absolutely required for anaphase spindle elongation.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C145 discuss how current findings relate to and refine prior work (Muscat et al., 2015; McNally et al., 2016; Laband et al., 2017). The reinterpretation that dynein's role in segregation is redundant (C143) is well-supported by the observation of mini anaphases. However, these are primarily interpretive claims reconciling current and prior work rather than new experimental findings.

results.result: Discussion of motor force balance: Rapid phenotypes upon dynein loss suggest it provides inward force. KLP-18 provides major outward force in C. elegans (versus kinesin-5 in other organisms). Prior work shows dynein and kinesin-5 antagonize each other in other systems, and kinesin-12 can provide supplemental outward force when kinesin-5 is inhibited.
results.evaluation: Claims C146-C149 and C151-C158 discuss force balance and compare motor roles across organisms, supported by citations to prior work (Ferenz et al., 2009; van Heesbeen et al., 2014; Wolff et al., 2021; Schuh and Ellenberg, 2007; Mann and Wadsworth, 2019; Mitchison et al., 2005; Tanenbaum et al., 2008, 2009; Vanneste et al., 2009). These provide important context but are primarily interpretive rather than new experimental findings.

results.result: Discussion of BMK-1 regulation: Aurora B kinase (AIR-2) is required for BMK-1 spindle localization and can phosphorylate BMK-1 in vitro. AIR-2 inhibition causes collapsed spindles, consistent with a role in regulating spindle force generation.
results.evaluation: Claims C159-C161 discuss potential regulation of BMK-1 by AIR-2, supported by citations to Bishop et al., 2005 and Divekar et al., 2021a. This represents discussion of prior work and speculation about mechanisms rather than new experimental findings from this study.

results.result: Discussion of pole protein functions: Not all pole protein depletions yield the same defects. ZYG-9 depletion causes multipolar spindles with broader defects, suggesting different groups of proteins work in parallel to form and stabilize poles rather than functioning as a single cross-linked network.
results.evaluation: Claims C166-C170 discuss recent work on ZYG-9 (Mullen et al., 2022) and interpret the broader implications for pole protein organization. The conclusion that different protein groups work in parallel (C170) is a reasonable inference but represents interpretation and discussion rather than new experimental data from this study.
